about: Hand-authored research inputs for tools/weapons/range_sim.py. The tool adds the computed sections (current game evaluation, reference physics, candidate fit, Godot cross-check cases) and writes data/weapons/range_research.json. Numbers are ranges [low, high] unless noted. Quality tags: primary-experimental (measured, published), primary-period (18th/19th c. text), secondary-reference (encyclopedia / museum / field manual), secondary-summary (read through a search abstract or a blog summary of the primary), estimate (derived here, see basis).

conventions.target: 0.5 m diameter disc (a torso) centred on the aim point, at launch height, flat ground
conventions.man_box: 0.5 m wide x 1.8 m tall box centred on the aim point
conventions.effective_range: D50: distance at which a trained user, standing still, aimed, full power, puts 50 % of shots into the 0.5 m disc
conventions.sure_hit_range: D100: every shot lands in the 0.5 m disc (game cone model) / about 95 % (Gaussian real-world)
conventions.max_range: longest carry on flat ground from 1.4 m at the best elevation (not an aimed range)
conventions.gaussian_to_disc: for a round-normal dispersion with per-axis sigma, P(r < a) = 1 - exp(-a^2 / (2 sigma^2)); D50 on a 0.25 m radius disc is where sigma = 0.212 m
conventions.game_cone_to_disc: Weapon.apply_spread draws r = tan(cone) * randf(): the miss radius is uniform on [0, d tan(cone)], so P(hit a 0.25 m disc) = min(1, 0.25 / (d tan cone)); D100 = 0.25 / tan(cone), D50 = 0.5 / tan(cone)

KRENN95.cite: Krenn, P., Kalaus, P., Hall, B. (1995). Material Culture and Military History: Test-Firing Early Modern Small Arms. Material History Review 42 (Fall 1995).
KRENN95.used_for: Graz Landeszeughaus firing of original 1571-c.1760 arms (1988-89): muzzle velocity 400-500 m/s for 10 of 13 guns (mean 454), ball deceleration about 2.5 m/s per metre over the first 24 m, accuracy on a 1.67 x 0.30 m target at 100 m (long arms) and 30 m (pistols), pistol hit rate 85 % and 99 %, wheellock pistol 9.54 g ball with 907 J at 8.5 m through a 2.8-3.0 mm breastplate, wound cavity 369 cm3 at 9 m vs 155 cm3 at 100 m (rifled flintlock STG 1288), Thierbach (1866) trial figures 60/40/25/20 % at 75/150/225/300 m. Per-weapon table values were images and not transcribed.

ROBINS1742.cite: Robins, B. (1742). New Principles of Gunnery. As summarised by the Australian Rock Art / arc.id.au page 'Benjamin Robins on Ballistics'.
ROBINS1742.used_for: ballistic-pendulum velocities of a 3/4 in, 1/12 lb musket ball: 1670, 1550 and 1425 ft/s at 25, 75 and 125 ft; drag about 120 x the ball's weight at ~1600 ft/s; true maximum range of such shot about half a mile

HANGER1814.cite: Hanger, G. (1814). To All Sportsmen, and Particularly to Farmers and Gamekeepers. London.
HANGER1814.used_for: a soldier's musket strikes a man's figure at 80 yd, perhaps 100; a man aimed at by a common musket at 150 yd is very unlucky to be hit, at 200 yd one might as well fire at the moon; riflemen told him they were confident of hitting a man's head at 200 yd; a rifleman lying prone fired at him and Tarleton from about 400 yards (18 Aug 1780) and killed a horse beside them

JAR2013.cite: Journal of the American Revolution (2013). How far is 'musket-shot'? Farther than you think.
JAR2013.used_for: period definitions of musket-shot: Lochee 1783 (300 yd, 200-250 yd with careless loading), Smith 1779 (point blank 300 yd, wounding to 360 yd), Simes 1776 (ordinary range 240 yd), Clairac 1773 (300 yd; smallest 160-200 yd)

JAR2017.cite: Journal of the American Revolution (2017). The prowess of American riflemen: a mystery now solved.
JAR2017.used_for: Hanger's 400-yard rifle shot (1780); Lancaster rifle about .50 bore, 36 balls to the pound, 3 ft 3 in barrel; riflemen needing two minutes or more per load against four or five musket shots a minute (the article's framing)

DUFFY_KK.cite: Kabinettskriege blog (2016), How accurate were regular soldiers in the mid-eighteenth century?, citing Duffy, C., The Army of Frederick the Great, p. 128 and The Military Experience in the Age of Reason, pp. 207-209.
DUFFY_KK.used_for: Winterfeldt trial 1755 (Prussian musket, large screen): 46 % hits at 150 paces, 16.6 % at 200, 10-13 % at 300; Chotusitz 1742: about 650,000 rounds for about 2,500 enemy dead and wounded (Mauvillon)

WP_BESS.used_for: .75 bore, 3.95-4.59 kg, 42-46 in barrel; muzzle velocity estimates disputed (Rogers 1,500 ft/s vs Harding); effective about 100 yd against point targets; 1841 Royal Engineers trial (poor beyond 150 yd)

WHN_BESS.cite: Warfare History Network, Revolutionary War Weapons: The Brown Bess Musket (page returned 403; figures from the search abstract).
WHN_BESS.used_for: 1841 Royal Engineers test: carry 100 to 700 yd depending on elevation, two muskets at the same elevation differing by up to 300 yd; at 150 yd 3 hits in 4 on a target twice as high and twice as broad as a man with very careful shooting; 0 hits in 10 at 250 yd

WP_CHARLEVILLE.used_for: .69 bore with .65 ball, 45 in barrel, 4.5 kg, 1,000-1,200 ft/s (300-370 m/s), effective about 100 yd against a man-sized target, 2-3 rounds a minute

WP_LONGRIFLE.used_for: .25-.62 calibre, .40-.48 most common, 1,200-1,600 ft/s (370-490 m/s), about 100 yd for average shooters, 200-300 yd for experts, slower to load than a musket

WP_PISTOLET1733.used_for: French cavalry flintlock pistol, .69 calibre, 310 mm barrel, 1.23 kg, effective range 5-10 m

MILKS19.cite: Milks, A., Parker, D., Pope, M. (2019). External ballistics of Pleistocene hand-thrown spears: experimental performance data and implications for human evolution. Scientific Reports 9: 820.
MILKS19.quality: primary-experimental (numbers via the project's throwables design doc, UCL/phys.org/The Conversation summaries and a blog digest)
MILKS19.used_for: six trained javelin athletes, Schoeningen replicas 760 and 800 g; release 11.8-20.1 m/s; hits out to 20 m, none at 25 m; accuracy best at 5 m and falling with distance; about 17 % hits at 10 m on one hay bale, 33 % with two stacked; 120 throws; distance throws 20 to a little over 30 m

MILKS20.cite: Milks, A. (2020). A Review of Ethnographic Use of Wooden Spears and Implications for Pleistocene Hominin Hunting. Open Quaternary 6: 12.
MILKS20.used_for: Tiwi experiment: nine throwers put a 1.8 kg spear 31.8-43.7 m without aiming; Tasmanian 242-845 g spears reported thrown 30-100 m (upper figures probably exaggerated)

CHURCHILL93.cite: Churchill, S. E. (1993). Weapon technology, prey size selection, and hunting methods in modern hunter-gatherers. Archeological Papers of the American Anthropological Association 4: 11-24.
CHURCHILL93.quality: secondary-summary (figures as cited by later papers)
CHURCHILL93.used_for: ethnographic mean effective distance of a hand-thrown spear about 7.8-8 m; bow (Kalahari) 25 m or less; atlatl about 40 m

BEB23.cite: Bebber, M. R., Buchanan, B., Eren, M. I., Walker, R. S., Zirkle, D. (2023). Atlatl use equalizes female and male projectile weapon velocity. Scientific Reports 13: 13349.
BEB23.used_for: 108 novices, 2,160 launches; 800 g javelin mean 9.8 m/s (men 8.1-16.1, women 5.1-11.5); 200 g atlatl dart mean 16.2 m/s (men 10.1-24.1, women 10.1-20.1)

WHIT17.cite: Whittaker, J. C., Pettigrew, D. B., Grohsmeyer, R. J. (2017). Atlatl Dart Velocity: Accurate Measurements and Implications for Paleoindian and Archaic Archaeology. PaleoAmerica 3(2): 161-181.
WHIT17.used_for: carefully measured darts mostly under 34-35 m/s; specialised equipment approaches 38 m/s

WHIT13.cite: Whittaker, J. C. (2013). Comparing Atlatls and Bows: Accuracy and Learning Curve. Ethnoarchaeology 5(2): 100-111.
WHIT13.used_for: bows are more consistent and more accurate than atlatls and easier to learn; top atlatl competitors score about 78 % of top archers' scores

WHIT24.cite: Whittaker, J. C., Pettigrew, D. B. (2024). Atlatl vs Bison on the Prehistoric Prairie. Rootstalk X(1).
WHIT24.used_for: darts 90-230 g at 54-60 mph (24-27 m/s); throws from 12 m, described as a typical hunting distance; good accuracy at 15-20 m; 106 J at impact; 30-46 cm penetration into bison

WP_ST.used_for: darts 1.2-2.7 m; can fly well over 100 m but are most accurate within about 20 m; replica exit speeds 20-30 m/s

GWR_ATLATL.cite: Guinness World Records, spear throwing (atlatl) distance: 258.63 m, David Engvall, Aurora, Colorado, 15 July 1995 (via search abstract).
GWR_ATLATL.used_for: specialised flight dart; far beyond a hunting dart's range

PONTZER17.cite: Pontzer, H., Raichlen, D. A., Basdeo, T., Harris, J. A., Mabulla, A. Z. P., Wood, B. M. (2017). Mechanics of archery among Hadza hunter-gatherers. Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports 16: 57-64.
PONTZER17.used_for: draw force 311 +- 98 N (about 70 lbf); arrow velocity 45.1 +- 7.0 m/s; arrow KE 36.9 +- 13.4 J; targets at 15, 30 and 50 m, chosen to match hunting shot distances

POPE1918.cite: Pope, S. T. (1918). Yahi Archery. University of California Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology 13(3).
POPE1918.used_for: Ishi's hunting bow under 40 lb, 1 oz hunting arrows; best flight shot 185 yd (Pope 200 yd with the same bow); 100 yd took about 4 s at a 30 degree loft; American Round (30 arrows at each distance, 48 in face): 19-23 hits at 40 yd, 17-20 at 50 yd, 10-13 at 60 yd; at 10-20 yd one or two of five arrows hit a 3-4 in object

POPE1923.cite: Pope, S. T. (1923). A Study of Bows and Arrows / Hunting with the Bow and Arrow.
POPE1923.used_for: light arrow from a 65 lb yew bow about 150 ft/s by stopwatch (search abstract); 68 lb bow put an arrow through a deer at 50 yd and it flew 20 yd on; deer shot at 75 yd with the arrow through the chest; grizzly at 60 yd

WP_LONGBOW.cite: Wikipedia, English longbow (citing Strickland & Hardy, Stretton, Loades).
WP_LONGBOW.used_for: Mary Rose replica of 150 lbf shot a 53.6 g arrow 328 m (359 yd with lighter arrows); Stretton: heavy war shafts at 47.23 m/s from a 144 lbf bow; war bows 100-185 lbf; the longbow left military use in the early 17th century; archery revived as a pastime in the late 18th century

FM3-23.30.cite: US Army FM 3-23.30 Grenades and Pyrotechnic Signals, ch. 1, sec. 1-5.
FM3-23.30.used_for: a 14 oz (397 g) M67 grenade: an average soldier throws the M67 about 35 m effectively (hand-throw speed analogue for a heavy thrown tool)

HA.cite: HatchetsandAxes.com guides: How to Throw a Tomahawk; Long Distance Tomahawk Throwing - 25 to 30+ Feet; Tomahawk Throwing Competitions.
HA.used_for: one turn from about 13-14 ft (5-6 paces); 18-20 ft for two turns; 25-28 ft for three turns is about the most thrown at a range; advanced competitors up to 30 ft; WATL throws from 12 and 15 ft

HAWK.used_for: one revolution from 5-6 steps, two to double that; long throws of 25 ft or more

W_TOM.cite: Wikipedia, Tomahawk (via the throwables design doc).
W_TOM.used_for: haft under 61 cm, head 260-570 g, edge rarely over 10 cm

MILLER79.cite: Miller, D. G., Bailey, A. B. (1979). Sphere drag at Mach numbers from 0.3 to 2.0 at Reynolds numbers approaching 10^7. Journal of Fluid Mechanics 93(3): 449-464. doi:10.1017/S0022112079002597
MILLER79.quality: primary-experimental (curve values approximated here; the paper was not read, only its abstract)
MILLER79.used_for: shape of the round-ball drag coefficient: about 0.5 subsonic, rising through the transonic region to about 1.0 at Mach 1.2-1.6; the analysis includes 18th-century firing data such as Hutton's (1787-1791)

PARK11.cite: Park, J. L. (2011). The aerodynamic drag and axial rotation of an arrow. Proc. IMechE Part P: J. Sports Engineering and Technology 225: 199-211.
PARK11.used_for: arrow drag is dominated by viscous shaft drag plus the point and fletching; used only to justify a quadratic drag constant of the order 0.001-0.003 per metre for a feathered wooden arrow

ARROW_LOSS.cite: Traditional-archery chronograph reports (Archery Talk / Traditional Bowhunter forums; search abstract): a hunting arrow loses about 2-4 ft/s per 10 yd; wood arrows from 42-70 lb longbows leave at 165-183 ft/s (50-56 m/s).
ARROW_LOSS.used_for: order of magnitude of arrow speed loss; cross-checked against Ishi's 185 yd flight shot

FLINT_MISFIRE.cite: British trials of the 1830s (Woolwich 1834 and an 1830 test of about 6,000 rounds) as reported on civilwartalk.com and in search summaries: flintlocks misfired about one shot in six, percussion about one in a thousand.
FLINT_MISFIRE.used_for: reliability context only; not a range figure

ROBERTS_BVM.cite: Roberts, N. A., Brown, J. W., Hammett, B., Kingston, P. D. F. A Detailed Study of the Effectiveness and Capabilities of 18th Century Musketry on the Battlefield (as summarised by the Bow Vs. Musket blog, 2019).
ROBERTS_BVM.used_for: a ball at 150 yd could pass through two soldiers; the study's maximum range claim (~1,200 m) is not used (it exceeds Robins' and the 1841 figures)

tomahawk.label: Thrown tomahawk / belt axe
tomahawk.period_fit: common 1750s frontier tool and weapon (design doc 1.2)
tomahawk.mass_basis: head 260-570 g on a haft under 61 cm [W_TOM]; a whole trade hatchet about 0.5-0.9 kg

release_speed_mps.basis: estimate: no measured tomahawk release speed was found. A sticking throw needs one turn per ~4.2 m at 4-9 m [HA]; the game's 9-14 m/s gives that spin budget. A hard, non-sticking throw is bounded by the 0.4 kg M67 analogue (35 m effective for an average soldier, i.e. ~18-19 m/s at 45 degrees) [FM3-23.30], lower for a heavier, tumbling axe

max_range_m.basis: estimate: 14 m/s gives ~21 m (reference model); a hard throw at 15-18 m/s gives ~25-33 m

effective_range_m.basis: competitive and practice sticking distances 12-30 ft (3.7-9 m) [HA][HAWK]; past ~9 m sticking needs a judged number of turns and is luck without practice at that exact distance

tomahawk.dispersion: experienced throwers group within a hand's width at 4-6 m; beyond ~9 m the error is mostly range (number of turns: blade or haft first) rather than line
tomahawk.lethality: only a blade-first strike cuts; 0.6 kg at 12 m/s carries ~43 J plus spin energy. Haft or poll strikes are blunt knocks. No penetration falloff worth modelling inside 15 m; the falloff is the stick chance
tomahawk.skill_fatigue: rotation control is the skill: under- or over-rotation by a quarter turn bounces it. Arm fatigue is minor for a few throws; holding the cocked pose is tiring after several seconds (the game's 3 s tremble is reasonable)

spear.label: Hand-thrown hunting spear / javelin
spear.period_fit: secondary 1750s weapon; iron trade point on a light shaft is plausible (design doc 1.1)
spear.mass_basis: Schoeningen replicas 760-800 g [MILKS19]; 800 g javelin [BEB23]; Tasmanian spears 242-845 g, Tiwi 1.8 kg [MILKS20]

release_speed_mps.basis: novice mean 9.8 m/s (men 8.1-16.1) [BEB23]; trained javelin athletes 11.8-20.1 m/s [MILKS19]

max_range_m.basis: distance throws of 760-800 g replicas 20 to a little over 30 m [MILKS19]; Tiwi 1.8 kg spears 31.8-43.7 m [MILKS20]; reference model 20 m/s -> ~42 m

effective_range_m.basis: ethnographic mean ~7.8 m [CHURCHILL93]; trained athletes hit out to 20 m but not 25 m, about 17-33 % at 10 m on hay bales [MILKS19]

spear.dispersion: accuracy best at 5 m and falls steadily; at 10 m roughly one throw in three to six hits a bale-sized target (trained, unhurried)
spear.lethality: heavy: 0.8 kg at 15-18 m/s gives 90-130 J with a long wound channel; drag is small, so the impact speed hardly falls inside 20 m. Lethality is limited by hitting, not by energy
spear.skill_fatigue: skill is a significant factor [MILKS19]; novices are ~half as fast [BEB23]. A heavy spear held cocked tires the arm within a few seconds

atlatl.label: Atlatl (spear-thrower) and dart
atlatl.period_fit: anachronistic in the 1750s eastern woodlands (replaced by the bow c. 500-1000 CE); the game's legendary relic (design doc 1.3)

release_speed_mps.basis: novice mean 16.2 m/s [BEB23]; 24-27 m/s with hunting darts [WHIT24]; carefully measured darts mostly under 34-35 m/s [WHIT17]

max_range_m.basis: over 100 m [WP_ST]; reference model 28-32 m/s -> ~70-95 m for a hunting dart; the 258.63 m record used a specialised flight dart [GWR_ATLATL]

effective_range_m.basis: 12 m described as a typical hunting distance, good accuracy at 15-20 m [WHIT24]; most accurate within ~20 m [WP_ST]; ethnographic hunting ~40 m [CHURCHILL93] (upper bound)

atlatl.dispersion: less consistent than a bow; top atlatl competitors score ~78 % of top archers' scores [WHIT13]
atlatl.lethality: 106 J at impact and 30-46 cm penetration into bison at 12 m [WHIT24]; darts keep most of their speed inside 30 m
atlatl.skill_fatigue: long learning curve (harder to master than the bow [WHIT13]); the dart leaves on a whip of the wrist, so a tired or rushed cast loses speed and line

bow.label: Hunting self bow (Eastern Woodlands) / English sporting longbow
bow.period_fit: Eastern Woodlands hunting bows still in use in the 1750s beside the trade musket; the English longbow was out of military use by the early 1600s and revived as a pastime in the 1780s [WP_LONGBOW]
bow.mass_basis: 1 oz (28 g) hunting arrows [POPE1918]; Hadza arrows ~36 g (from 36.9 J at 45.1 m/s) [PONTZER17]; English war arrows 54-96 g [WP_LONGBOW]

release_speed_mps.basis: Hadza 45.1 +- 7.0 m/s at ~70 lbf [PONTZER17]; 65 lb yew with a light arrow ~150 ft/s = 46 m/s [POPE1923]; 42-70 lb longbows 165-183 ft/s = 50-56 m/s [ARROW_LOSS]; 144 lbf war bow heavy shaft 47 m/s [WP_LONGBOW]

max_range_m.basis: Ishi's <40 lb bow 185 yd (169 m), Pope 200 yd (183 m) [POPE1918]; 150 lbf Mary Rose replica 328 m with a 53.6 g arrow [WP_LONGBOW]

effective_range_m.basis: Kalahari bow hunting 25 m or less [CHURCHILL93]; Hadza practise at 15-50 m [PONTZER17]; Ishi: 63-77 % on a 48 in face at 40 yd but ~18 % on a 0.5 m disc by the same dispersion, so D50 on a torso ~20 m for him; Pope killed deer at 50-75 yd with a 68 lb bow (exceptional)

bow.dispersion: Ishi (a hunter, not a target archer): sigma ~0.05 m at 14 m (~4 mrad) and ~0.39 m at 37 m (~10 mrad) [POPE1918]; a practised modern traditional archer ~2-4 mrad
bow.lethality: a broadhead kills by cutting, so lethality barely depends on distance inside the aimed range: 37 J (Hadza) is enough for pass-throughs on deer at 45 m [POPE1923]. Arrows lose only ~10-15 % of speed over 50 m
bow.skill_fatigue: full draw can only be held a few seconds before the aim shakes (the game's 2.5 s start is right for a 50-70 lb bow); rapid shooting from the bow hand is period-correct; archery skill takes years but is easier than the atlatl [WHIT13]

pistol.label: Smoothbore flintlock pistol (horse / belt pistol)
pistol.period_fit: carried by officers, cavalry and some frontiersmen; always a close-quarters weapon
pistol.mass_basis: .56-.69 ball: about 15-30 g (a .69 ball is ~31 g); Graz wheellock pistol 9.54 g [KRENN95]

release_speed_mps.basis: modern replicas with light loads ~600-850 ft/s (forum reports, low quality); Graz pistol with a full charge (1/3 of ball weight) delivered 907 J at 8.5 m with a 9.54 g ball, i.e. ~436 m/s [KRENN95]

max_range_m.basis: reference model (Graz-fitted ball drag): a 23 g .62 ball at 200-220 m/s carries ~590-620 m at ~32 degrees; no measured pistol max range was found

effective_range_m.basis: from a rest the Graz pistols put 85-99 % on a 0.30 m wide target at 30 m [KRENN95]; one-handed offhand in a fight the period effective range is 5-10 m (French 1733 cavalry pistol) [WP_PISTOLET1733]

pistol.dispersion: short sight radius, heavy trigger and one-handed hold: several times the rested dispersion; ~6-10 mrad offhand
pistol.lethality: a big soft ball is lethal at any range it can be aimed at; 907 J at 8.5 m defeated a 3 mm breastplate [KRENN95]
pistol.skill_fatigue: a heavy (1.2 kg) pistol held out one-handed wavers within seconds; reload is as long as a musket's per shot

musket.label: Smoothbore flintlock musket (Brown Bess / Charleville)
musket.period_fit: the standard military and trade long arm of the 1750s
musket.mass_basis: .65-.71 service ball about 25-32 g; Robins' 1/12 lb ball 37.8 g [ROBINS1742]; Graz STG 1318 31 g [KRENN95]

release_speed_mps.basis: Charleville 300-370 m/s [WP_CHARLEVILLE]; Graz 400-500 m/s, mean 454 [KRENN95]; Robins 1670 ft/s (509 m/s) at 25 ft [ROBINS1742]

decay.graz: about 2.5 m/s lost per metre in the first 24 m [KRENN95]
decay.energy_100m: about 1/3 to 1/2 of the muzzle energy remains at 100 m

max_range_m.basis: 1841 Royal Engineers: 100-700 yd depending on elevation, two muskets at one elevation differing by up to 300 yd [WHN_BESS]; Robins: true maximum about half a mile (~800 m) [ROBINS1742]; the reference model gives 760-830 m for 320-454 m/s with the Graz-fitted drag; period 'musket-shot' of 240-300 yd was an engagement distance, not a limit [JAR2013]

effective_range_m.basis: man's figure at 80-100 yd, hopeless at 200 yd [HANGER1814]; 3 in 4 on a double-size man at 150 yd with very careful shooting, 0/10 at 250 yd [WHN_BESS]; ~50 % on a 1.67 x 0.30 m target at 100 m from a rest [KRENN95]; volley trials 60/40/25/20 % at 75/150/225/300 m on a large target [KRENN95]; 46 % at 150 paces, 16.6 % at 200 [DUFFY_KK]

musket.dispersion: sigma ~2 mrad from a rest with a careful load (Graz), ~3-4 mrad standing with service loads (1841 test); a loose ball also wanders (Robins observed curving paths)
musket.lethality: ~3 kJ at the muzzle; about 1/3-1/2 of it left at 100 m; still lethal at 300 m (a spent ball at ~150-180 m/s breaks bone); a ball at 150 yd could pass through two men [ROBERTS_BVM]; wound cavity 530 cm3 at 9 m (STG 1318) and 155 cm3 at 100 m for the rifled STG 1288 [KRENN95]
musket.skill_fatigue: a 4.5 kg musket held at the aim wavers within seconds (period drill did not hold the aim); fouling slows loading after 20-30 shots; flints misfire roughly one shot in six [FLINT_MISFIRE]; skill mostly shows in loading speed (3-4 rounds a minute drilled)

rifle.label: Pennsylvania (long) rifle - reference only
rifle.period_fit: frontier hunting rifle from the early 1700s; not in the current loadout
rifle.mass_basis: .45-.50 patched ball 8-13 g; Lancaster rifle 36 balls to the pound (12.6 g) [JAR2017]

max_range_m.basis: reference model: 12.6 g .50 ball at 450 m/s -> ~660 m (Graz-fitted drag) to ~780 m (Robins-fitted)

effective_range_m.basis: average shooters ~100 yd, experts 200-300 yd [WP_LONGRIFLE]; riflemen claimed a man's head at 200 yd, a near miss on Hanger at 400 yd [HANGER1814]

rifle.dispersion: sigma ~0.5-1 mrad for a practised shooter from a rest
rifle.lethality: smaller ball (12 g) but faster and tighter; kills deer at 150-200 m
rifle.skill_fatigue: patched ball: ~1 aimed shot a minute or slower (JAR2017's two or more minutes is the slow end); the edge is the marksman, not the gun

ladder_targets.about: Consensus targets for the balance step, chosen from the research ranges above. D50/D100 are for the game's cone model (uniform miss radius) on a 0.5 m disc, trained user standing still, fully aimed, full power. steady_d50 is the braced/RMB or crouched best case. max_range is from 1.4 m on flat ground. launch speed is the full-power speed. Order: tomahawk < spear < atlatl < bow (thrown and drawn) and pistol << musket < rifle (firearms); a firearm's effective range beats every bow and thrown weapon except that the pistol sits with the atlatl/bow.

tomahawk.note: the current range (20 m) is right; its 0.5 deg cone hits every time out to the full reach. Keep the spin-assist window (2.5-15 m) as the sticking range: past ~9 m sticking should become unreliable

spear.note: a 20 m hit should be a lucky throw (the Milks athletes hit nothing at 25 m); 22 m/s is above the measured 20.1 m/s ceiling

atlatl.note: faster and flatter than the spear, less consistent than the bow

bow.note: gravity must be 9.8 like everything else: with g = 5 and no drag the bow out-ranges the pistol (770 m); 62 m/s is a 150 lb war bow with a light arrow

pistol.note: honestly short in aimed range (below the bow past ~20 m) but far more lethal inside it

musket.note: a smoothbore: the current 0.15 deg (0.037 deg crouched + steady) is expert-rifle accuracy; the long range comes from the ball's reach and lethality, not pinpoint accuracy

rifle.note: reference for a future rifle; the over-under uses musket-class smoothbore barrels

reference_bodies.about: Real-world flight model used only for comparison (quadratic drag, g = 9.81, air 1.2 kg/m3, sound 340 m/s). Round balls use a Mach-dependent sphere Cd approximated from MILLER79, scaled x1.25 so the ball loses 2.5 m/s per metre near the muzzle as in the Graz tests (KRENN95); that scale also lands Robins' ball within ~8 % of his 'half a mile' (x1.0 matches his pendulum velocities to 2 % but over-ranges by ~28 %). The others use a constant drag area (estimate).

tomahawk.basis: tumbling haft ~0.45 x 0.03 m side-on, Cd ~1, averaged with end-on: CdA ~0.006 m2 (estimate)

spear.basis: 2.3 m x 30 mm shaft, skin friction plus point: CdA ~0.001-0.0015 m2 (estimate)

atlatl.basis: 1.8 m x 12 mm fletched dart: CdA ~0.0003-0.0005 m2 (estimate)

bow.basis: feathered wooden broadhead arrow: CdA chosen so the quadratic constant k = rho CdA / 2m = 0.0024 per m (2-4 ft/s lost per 10 yd [ARROW_LOSS]; Ishi's 185 yd check below)
